theory.intro: Instead of reading a graph, this skill works the other way around: given a description of how a quantity changes, you build the matching graph. The idea is the same either way — a straight piece means a constant rate, and a curved piece means a changing rate — but now you decide the shape before it exists.
facts: For a container filled at a constant rate, a **narrow** cross-section makes the height rise **quickly** (steep), and a **wide** cross-section makes the height rise **slowly** (flat).
A container with a **constant** cross-section (like a cylinder) gives a **straight** height-versus-time graph.
When a scenario has several stages, each stage becomes its own piece of the graph, joined in order at the time each stage ends.

Real quantities cannot jump instantly between values unless something physically instantaneous happens (like a tank being suddenly refilled) — a smooth change in behaviour should usually be drawn as a smooth curve, not a sharp corner.
steps: Identify each stage of the scenario, in time order.
For each stage, decide whether the quantity increases, decreases, or stays constant.
For each stage, decide whether the rate is constant (straight) or changing (curved, and if so getting steeper or flatter).
Draw each stage as the matching straight or curved piece, joined in order, with axes labelled.

foundation.solution_text:
$A$ is correct.
The container has a constant cross-section, so the water height rises at a constant rate — a straight line.

$C$ is correct.
Near the bottom the container is narrow, so the height rises quickly at first; near the top it is wide, so the height rises more and more slowly — a curve that rises but gets flatter.

$B$ is correct.
A real car's speed cannot jump instantly between values, so it must slow down and speed up smoothly through the corner, giving a smooth curved dip rather than a sharp point ($A$) or a sudden step ($C$).

$A$ is correct.
A jumping body follows smooth, rounded arcs under gravity, not sharp triangular peaks, so the graph should be made of smooth rounded humps rather than the sharp zigzags in $B$ and $C$.

development.solution_text:
$B$ is correct.
Near the bottom of the sphere the container is narrow, so the height rises quickly; in the middle it is widest, so the height rises most slowly; then as it narrows again near the top, the height speeds up again. This slow–fast–slow pattern gives a curve that rises, gets steeper, then gets flatter again — not the flat line in $A$ or the straight line in $C$.

Story 1 matches Graph $X$: the level stays constant, so the graph is a flat horizontal line above zero.
Story 2 matches Graph $Y$: the cost rises at a constant rate from zero, so the graph is a straight line starting at the origin.
Story 3 matches Graph $Z$: the wax burns down at a constant rate, giving a straight falling line, and then stays at zero once it is used up.

The student's reasoning only works when the container's cross-section stays the same width all the way up.
This container is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, so the water height rises quickly at first (through the narrow part) and then more and more slowly (through the wide part).
The correct graph should be a curve that starts steep and gets flatter — increasing at a decreasing rate — not a straight line.

mastery.solution_text:
The student's graph rises quickly at first and then flattens off — that would be correct for a container that is narrow at the bottom and wide at the top, the opposite of this one.
This container is wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so the water height should rise slowly at first (while the wide base fills) and then more and more quickly as the narrow top fills.
The correct graph should rise slowly at first and then get steeper — increasing at an increasing rate — the reverse of the curve the student drew.
